verses.text: Abimelech the son of Jerubbaal went to Shechem to his mother’s brothers, and spoke with them, and with all the family of the house of his mother’s father, saying,

“Please speak in the ears of all the men of Shechem, ‘Is it better for you that all the sons of Jerubbaal, who are seventy persons, rule over you, or that one rule over you?’ Remember also that I am your bone and your flesh.”
His mother’s brothers spoke of him in the ears of all the men of Shechem all these words. Their hearts inclined to follow Abimelech; for they said, “He is our brother.”
They gave him seventy pieces of silver out of the house of Baal Berith, with which Abimelech hired vain and light fellows, who followed him.
He went to his father’s house at Ophrah, and killed his brothers the sons of Jerubbaal, being seventy persons, on one stone: but Jotham the youngest son of Jerubbaal was left; for he hid himself.
All the men of Shechem assembled themselves together, and all the house of Millo, and went and made Abimelech king, by the oak of the pillar that was in Shechem.
When they told it to Jotham, he went and stood on the top of Mount Gerizim, and lifted up his voice, cried out, and said to them, “Listen to me, you men of Shechem, that God may listen to you.
The trees set out to anoint a king over themselves. They said to the olive tree, ‘Reign over us.’
“But the olive tree said to them, ‘Should I stop producing my oil, with which they honor God and man by me, and go to wave back and forth over the trees?’
“The trees said to the fig tree, ‘Come and reign over us.’
“But the fig tree said to them, ‘Should I leave my sweetness, and my good fruit, and go to wave back and forth over the trees?’
“The trees said to the vine, ‘Come and reign over us.’
“The vine said to them, ‘Should I leave my new wine, which cheers God and man, and go to wave back and forth over the trees?’
“Then all the trees said to the bramble, ‘Come and reign over us.’
“The bramble said to the trees, ‘If in truth you anoint me king over you, then come and take refuge in my shade; and if not, let fire come out of the bramble, and devour the cedars of Lebanon.’

“Now therefore, if you have dealt truly and righteously, in that you have made Abimelech king, and if you have dealt well with Jerubbaal and his house, and have done to him according to the deserving of his hands
(for my father fought for you, and risked his life, and delivered you out of the hand of Midian;

and you have risen up against my father’s house today, and have slain his sons, seventy persons, on one stone, and have made Abimelech, the son of his female servant, king over the men of Shechem, because he is your brother);
if you then have dealt truly and righteously with Jerubbaal and with his house today, then rejoice in Abimelech, and let him also rejoice in you;
but if not, let fire come out from Abimelech, and devour the men of Shechem, and the house of Millo; and let fire come out from the men of Shechem, and from the house of Millo, and devour Abimelech.”
Jotham ran away, and fled, and went to Beer,  and lived there, for fear of Abimelech his brother.
Abimelech was prince over Israel three years.
Then God sent an evil spirit between Abimelech and the men of Shechem; and the men of Shechem dealt treacherously with Abimelech,

that the violence done to the seventy sons of Jerubbaal might come, and that their blood might be laid on Abimelech their brother, who killed them, and on the men of Shechem, who strengthened his hands to kill his brothers.
The men of Shechem set an ambush for him on the tops of the mountains, and they robbed all who came along that way by them, and Abimelech was told about it.
Gaal the son of Ebed came with his brothers, and went over to Shechem; and the men of Shechem put their trust in him.
They went out into the field, harvested their vineyards, trod the grapes, held festival, and went into the house of their god, and ate and drank, and cursed Abimelech.

Gaal the son of Ebed said, “Who is Abimelech, and who is Shechem, that we should serve him? Isn’t he the son of Jerubbaal? Isn’t Zebul his officer? Serve the men of Hamor the father of Shechem, but why should we serve him?
I wish that this people were under my hand! Then I would remove Abimelech.” He said to Abimelech, “Increase your army, and come out!”
When Zebul the ruler of the city heard the words of Gaal the son of Ebed, his anger burned.
He sent messengers to Abimelech craftily, saying, “Behold, Gaal the son of Ebed and his brothers have come to Shechem; and behold, they incite the city against you.
Now therefore, go up by night, you and the people who are with you, and lie in wait in the field.

It shall be that in the morning, as soon as the sun is up, you shall rise early, and rush on the city. Behold, when he and the people who are with him come out against you, then may you do to them as you shall find occasion.”
Abimelech rose up, and all the people who were with him, by night, and they laid wait against Shechem in four companies.
Gaal the son of Ebed went out, and stood in the entrance of the gate of the city. Abimelech rose up, and the people who were with him, from the ambush.
When Gaal saw the people, he said to Zebul, “Behold, people are coming down from the tops of the mountains.” Zebul said to him, “You see the shadow of the mountains as if they were men.”
Gaal spoke again and said, “Behold, people are coming down by the middle of the land, and one company comes by the way of the oak of Meonenim.”
Then Zebul said to him, “Now where is your mouth, that you said, ‘Who is Abimelech, that we should serve him?’ Isn’t this the people that you have despised? Please go out now and fight with them.”
Gaal went out before the men of Shechem, and fought with Abimelech.
Abimelech chased him, and he fled before him, and many fell wounded, even to the entrance of the gate.
Abimelech lived at Arumah; and Zebul drove out Gaal and his brothers, that they should not dwell in Shechem.
On the next day, the people went out into the field; and they told Abimelech.
He took the people, and divided them into three companies, and laid wait in the field; and he looked, and behold, the people came out of the city. So, he rose up against them, and struck them.
Abimelech and the companies that were with him rushed forward, and stood in the entrance of the gate of the city; and the two companies rushed on all who were in the field, and struck them.
Abimelech fought against the city all that day; and he took the city, and killed the people in it. He beat down the city, and sowed it with salt.
When all the men of the tower of Shechem heard of it, they entered into the stronghold of the house of Elberith.
Abimelech was told that all the men of the tower of Shechem were gathered together.

Abimelech went up to Mount Zalmon, he and all the people who were with him; and Abimelech took an ax in his hand, and cut down a bough from the trees, and took it up, and laid it on his shoulder. Then he said to the people who were with him, “What you have seen me do, make haste, and do as I have done!”

All the people likewise each cut down his bough, and followed Abimelech, and put them at the base of the stronghold, and set the stronghold on fire on them; so that all the people of the tower of Shechem died also, about a thousand men and women.
Then Abimelech went to Thebez, and encamped against Thebez, and took it.
But there was a strong tower within the city, and all the men and women of the city fled there, and shut themselves in, and went up to the roof of the tower.
Abimelech came to the tower, and fought against it, and came near to the door of the tower to burn it with fire.
A certain woman cast an upper millstone on Abimelech’s head, and broke his skull.
Then he called hastily to the young man his armor bearer, and said to him, “Draw your sword, and kill me, that men not say of me, ‘A woman killed him.’ His young man thrust him through, and he died.”
When the men of Israel saw that Abimelech was dead, they each departed to his place.
Thus God repaid the wickedness of Abimelech, which he did to his father, in killing his seventy brothers;
and God repaid all the wickedness of the men of Shechem on their heads; and the curse of Jotham the son of Jerubbaal came on them.

footnotes.content: Abimelech begins with flattery and family ties, a careful dance to make murder look reasonable. How often we dress up ambition in the language of kinship, hoping those closest to us won't see what's really in our heart.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He reminds them they share blood, then poses his poisoned question: one rule or seventy? He already knows what fear and self-interest will answer. Grace never builds on these foundations, yet here Abimelech does.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Their hearts inclined—that word troubles me. How easily we drift when someone speaks what we wished to hear. They called him brother, but a true brother would not ask them to buy his rule with silver and blood.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Seventy pieces of silver from Baal Berith's house—they bought hired men to do what no honest heart should do. The house of the covenant became the paymaster for murder. Money can corrupt even the holy places we build.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Seventy brothers slain on one stone—the number echoes, deliberate and brutal. Jotham alone escapes; the Lord hides him. In the darkest hour, escape is itself a grace we might not yet understand.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: By the oak of the pillar they crowned him—trees witness; stones remember. Even as they did this, creation bore testimony that this kingdom was not of God. A true covenant needs no such crown.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jotham climbed Mount Gerizim to cry out his parable. One voice against a city, one young man speaking truth alone—I think he knew God would listen even if Shechem would not.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The trees decide to crown a king—Jotham's parable opens gently, like a door. We recognize this story because we live it daily: the foolish who think they need rulers to give them purpose.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The olive tree asks: Should I stop making oil that honors God and man? There's wisdom in this tree—it knows its calling and sees that true greatness lies in faithful work, not in waves and ruling.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The fig tree is asked next—each tree that declines helps us see the pattern. The good refuse the crown because they know what matters: steadfast fruitfulness, not authority.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Should I leave my sweetness and my good fruit? The fig tree speaks with a question, not a rebuke. It simply names what it would lose—and somehow that quiet refusal is more powerful than any anger.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The vine is asked—three good things now have said no. The pattern is teaching us something. When enough voices refuse, we begin to see what Jotham already knows: there's no worthy choice here.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The vine's answer echoes the others—my new wine cheers God and man. Each tree names one gift it cannot abandon. Together they show us: faithfulness to your calling is better than any crown.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Then the trees ask the bramble—we know what's coming now. The good have all said no. The parable is turning toward the bitter truth: when honor goes begging, it falls to the worthless.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The bramble will reign and bring fire—this is the kingdom of ambition. It offers shelter but carries threat. Jotham's parable speaks directly to Abimelech: a usurper must rule by fear, and fear burns everything it touches.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jotham turns now to the plain judgment: Have you dealt truly and righteously? The word 'truly' carries weight—it calls for honesty in a moment when lies are most useful. Truth sees what was done.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: For my father fought for you, risked his life, delivered you—Jotham names Gideon's actual faithfulness, held it up like a mirror. He does not speak in anger, but in sorrow that they have forgotten so quickly.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: You have risen up against my father's house and made the servant's son king—Jotham names the truth plainly. Yet even in his witness, there's no cursing or retreat. He stands and speaks and then will run.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: If you have dealt truly and righteously, then rejoice—a condition so unlikely, so impossible, that the 'if' becomes almost gentle. Jotham is making room for repentance even as he knows what will come.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: But if not, let fire come out—Jotham pronounces the curse, yet his words are not dark magic; they are prophecy. The fire will come from Abimelech and Shechem turning on each other, the natural fruit of their own seeds.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jotham ran away and lived in Beer for fear of his brother—there is no shame in his flight. He has spoken truth at great cost; now he trusts his life to the Lord. Courage sometimes looks like running.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Abimelech was prince over Israel three years—a short reign, built on murder and silver. How quickly power rises when it is not rooted in righteousness, and how quickly it crumbles.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: God sent an evil spirit between them—the Lord does not author evil, but He allows it to work where hearts have already turned from Him. Even in judgment, God's hand is present; we reap what we have sown.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: That the violence might be avenged and blood laid on them—the seventy brothers cry out, and God hears. Their blood, spilled in one day on one stone, will not be forgotten. Justice waits, but it comes.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The men of Shechem set ambushes on the mountains—the kingdom that crowned him now begins to devour him. Greed and fear breed only suspicion; those who built on lies cannot trust each other.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Gaal the son of Ebed came to Shechem—a new man arrives, and the people place their hope in him as quickly as they did in Abimelech. This is the nature of a people who have forgotten how to look to God.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They harvested grapes, held festival, and cursed Abimelech—they took joy where they could and spoke their anger openly now. It is a small freedom, bitter and temporary, but people grasped at it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Gaal asks: Who is Abimelech? Why should we serve him?—it sounds almost like a call to freedom, but it is only a change of masters. Gaal offers no better path; he offers only his own ambition wrapped in different words.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: I wish this people were under my hand—Gaal reveals himself instantly. He speaks like a liberator but thinks like a tyrant. How easily we mistake new tyranny for freedom when we do not know what true liberty looks like.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Zebul heard these words and his anger burned—the officer sees his power slipping away. In a house built on violence, there is no loyalty, only competing ambitions and fear.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Zebul sent word to Abimelech craftily—he plays broker between rivals, offering his master intelligence in exchange for power. This is how kingdoms built on violence tear themselves apart.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Go up by night and lay in wait—war and ambush, the language of men who cannot lead openly or speak truth. The night hides their faces but not their intentions.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Rise early and rush on the city—Zebul coaches Abimelech like a theater director, orchestrating violence with careful timing. There's a sickness here: the calculation of cruelty.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Abimelech and his men rose up by night in four companies—the machinery of war grinds forward. Each man obeys, each plays his part in a story none of them truly controls anymore.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Gaal stood at the gate entrance as Abimelech rose from ambush—the moment of exposure. All of Gaal's bold words vanish when the truth appears before him in armed companies.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Gaal saw people coming down from the mountains—fear plays tricks on the eyes. Zebul mocks him: you see shadows as men. What he sees are his own empty promises made flesh, returned to haunt him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Gaal speaks again, insisting it is really men—his bravado crumbles, but he keeps talking, as though words can stop what is coming. Some men argue even as the ax falls.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Zebul mocks him: Now where is your mouth?—he throws Gaal's own words back at him. It is a cruel mercy: Gaal must watch his talk become action before his eyes.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Gaal went out and fought with Abimelech—he has no choice now. The man who promised liberation must face the tyrant he challenged. Pride moves him forward; wisdom has already fled.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Abimelech chased him, and many fell wounded at the gate—the brief battle is over quickly. Gaal's dream dies before Shechem's gate. A man's words can promise much; the sword decides truth.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Abimelech lived at Arumah and Zebul drove Gaal out—each man retreats to his own place. The city is quieter now, but not healed. Trust is shattered; Shechem is a house divided against itself.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The next day, people went out to the field—still the city moves, still they work, but now they are watched. Fear has become their daily bread.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He divided them into three companies and laid wait—Abimelech is relentless. Each act of rebellion is crushed before it can take root. A tyrant's grip only tightens.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Two companies rushed on all in the field and struck them—the slaughter is methodical. The city that once crowned a king watches its people fall, and learns a terrible lesson about the price of ambition.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He beat down the city and sowed it with salt—salt on the ruins means: let nothing grow here. It is a gesture of utter contempt, a scar written into the earth itself. Yet salt cannot stop the Lord's judgment from falling on him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The men of the tower heard and entered the stronghold—survival, that primal urge, gathers them together one last time. They flee into the house of Elberith, where once they paid silver for a crown.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Abimelech was told all men of the tower were gathered—he senses the trap that will be his ending, yet he moves toward it. Some men cannot stop until the Lord stops them.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Abimelech went to Mount Zalmon and cut a bough—he gathers branches as siege weapons, oddly mimicking nature even as he wages war. There is a dark poetry here: the bramble who would rule must harvest wood to burn his enemies.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Each man cut a bough and set the stronghold on fire—a thousand men and women perished in that tower, in that house of Baal Berith where once they bought power with silver. Justice comes through fire.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Abimelech went to Thebez and encamped against it—after Shechem, he moves to another city, carrying his hunger for dominion. He does not know he approaches his ending.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A strong tower stood in the city—refuge for the people of Thebez, as it was for Shechem's remnant. Towers are small kingdoms of stone; inside them men gather and wait and hope.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Abimelech came to the tower and fought against it—he means to burn this one too. Fire is his way; it has worked before. Yet this time the tower holds something different.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A certain woman cast an upper millstone on Abimelech's head and broke his skull—a woman's hand delivers the blow that ends him. She uses the tool of her livelihood; the millstone that grinds grain grinds the tyrant's pride to dust.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He called to his armor bearer: Draw your sword and kill me—even in death, Abimelech cares for his reputation. Pride dies last; the body falls, but the ego still grasps for a better story.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: When the men of Israel saw Abimelech was dead, they departed to his place—the kingdom dissolves. It held together only by force; without the tyrant, there is nothing left to bind them.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Thus God repaid the wickedness of Abimelech, which he did to his father by killing his seventy brothers—the account is settled. Murder returns to the murderer; what he sowed, he reaped. The Lord does not wink at blood.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: God repaid all the wickedness of Shechem and the curse of Jotham came on them—looking back from a longer road, I see how the Lord upholds His word. The faithful voice crying from the mountain found its hearing in time. As of 2026-10, I marvel how He never lets wrong speech pass unchecked, yet always leaves room for those who will listen.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
